raw_text:
Meet Steve
Steve Santarsiero represents the 10th Senatorial District in the Pennsylvania Senate, where he is a leading advocate for the environment, economic development, education, and infrastructure investment. Steve serves as Democratic Chair of the State Government Committee and as a member of the Judiciary; Consumer Protection & Professional Licensure; Institutional Sustainability & Innovation; and Rules & Executive Nominations Committees. He also serves in Senate Democratic Leadership as Caucus Secretary.
In Harrisburg, Steve has built a reputation for pragmatic, problem-solving leadership. He led the effort to pass Kayden’s Law (Act 8 of 2024), a bipartisan measure that strengthens protections for children in contentious custody disputes. Steve believes good policy starts by listening to the community and working across the aisle to get results in a divided legislature.
Steve is also a strong supporter of economic development in Bucks County. He has championed the growth of the Pennsylvania Biotechnology Center in Buckingham Township and supports initiatives like PA Innovate to strengthen our region’s life sciences economy. Thrombolex, a biotechnology company started in Bucks County that received state funding with Steve’s support, has saved over 2,000 lives with their BASHIR Endovascular Catheter. He has also supported the redevelopment of the North Point Keystone Trade Center on the former U.S. Steel property in Falls Township, transforming an abandoned industrial site into a major logistics and commercial hub while addressing long-standing environmental concerns from old industrial pollution at the site.
Steve believes we do not have to choose between affordable energy, a strong economy, and protecting our natural resources in the 10th Senate District. He introduced the Pennsylvania Reliable Energy Sustainability Standard (PRESS) to modernize the state’s energy portfolio standards, promote clean energy technologies, support energy jobs, and strengthen grid reliability while reducing carbon emissions.
As a former teacher, education remains a core priority. Steve is the author of legislation to create bell-to-bell cell phone-free classrooms in Pennsylvania’s K–12 schools. The bill passed the Senate with overwhelming bipartisan support and aims to help students stay focused and engaged in learning.
Steve is a strong advocate for public safety and first responders. Steve is the author of a bill to ban assault weapons, which he has introduced every year that he has been in the Senate. He also introduced Bryan’s Law to provide post-traumatic stress injury (PTSI) death benefits to emergency and law enforcement personnel. The bill is named for Pennsylvania State Trooper and former Green Beret Bryan F. Gray from Lower Makefield Township, who died by suicide as a result of trauma related to his service.
Steve believes leadership means showing up both in moments of celebration and in times of crisis. He is a tireless advocate for state investments in the 10th Senate District, delivering essential grants for local infrastructure improvements, arts and cultural institutions, economic development, and our parks. Steve is proud to spotlight the outstanding work happening across the district and to ensure municipalities and community organizations have the resources they need to succeed.
Steve also works to ensure communities receive the support they need in moments of crisis. Following a jet fuel pipeline leak in the Mt. Eyre neighborhood in Upper Makefield Township in 2025, he worked with residents and the township to urge the polluter, Sunoco-Energy Transfer, to fully clean the spill and restore resident drinking wells. Through that process, Steve identified weaknesses in Pennsylvania’s law. With his friend State Representative Perry Warren, he introduced the Environmental Clean Up and Responsibility Act (ECRA). If passed, this legislation would empower the Department of Environmental Protection to begin cleanup immediately after residential spills and hold polluters financially accountable.
Before his election to the Senate, then Attorney General Josh Shapiro appointed Steve in 2017 as Pennsylvania’s first Chief Deputy Attorney General for Environmental Protection. In that role, he oversaw the prosecution of environmental crimes and led Pennsylvania’s efforts to challenge federal rollbacks of environmental protections.
From 2008 to 2016, Steve represented the Yardley-Newtown area in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, where he earned a reputation in Harrisburg as a reformer and leader on education, infrastructure investment, environmental protection, and gun violence prevention. Back home in Bucks County, Steve led efforts to improve the resiliency of PECO’s electric grid, and successfully advocated for the jobs of thousands of Bucks County residents who work in New Jersey when that state enacted a public-sector residency requirement.
Steve’s path to public service began locally. After helping lead a grassroots effort to stop a proposed big-box mall in Lower Makefield Township, he ran for township supervisor and was elected in 2003. As a supervisor, he worked across party lines to improve transparency, address traffic challenges, and preserve open space.
Steve considers public service a calling. After witnessing the September 11th attacks from his office in Newark, New Jersey, he decided to leave the practice of law to pursue a new career in teaching. He earned his teaching certification at night from Holy Family University and became a social studies teacher at Bensalem High School, helping students develop a strong understanding of history and civics.
Steve earned his B.A. from Tufts University, his J.D. from the University of Pennsylvania Law School, and his M.Ed. from Holy Family University.
Steve and his wife, Ronni, have lived in Lower Makefield for over 30 years and have three grown children: Nancy, Bill, and John.

Delaware River Basin Commission) in which Republican state senators were challenging the DRBC's ban on fracking in the Delaware River Basin. Introduction
There has been a
steep decline in mental health
in children since the early 2010s. Kids are more depressed, anxious, and lonely than ever before. Their
academic performance is suffering
. There are more instances of
cyberbullying
and other behavioral issues during school hours. Teachers, parents, and students are
exhausted physically
, emotionally, and mentally.
This decline in our children’s mental health, social skills, and academic performance directly correlates to the rise of smartphones and social media apps. Many parents and teachers alike see the devastating impact these devices are having on our children and are asking for help. About
two thirds of Americans say all-day cellphone bans during school hours would improve students’ social skills, grades, and behavior
in class.
Our students deserve the opportunity to learn without a constant distraction in their pockets, and our bipartisan
legislation
will give them that opportunity.
Summary
To address a root cause of the mental health and academic decline experienced by Pennsylvania students, we have introduced
Senate Bill 1014
to require schools to adopt and implement a policy that prohibits the use of phones during the school day.  Exceptions would be made for:
Students with medical conditions,
Students with individualized education plans that require the use of a personal communication device,
English as a second language learners who use cellphones for translation purposes, and
Very limited instances for teachers who want to use cellphones as instructional tools with approval by the school principal.
If enacted, Pennsylvania would join 27 states in restricting these devices including New York, Virginia, and Florida, 18 of which have bell-to-bell bans.
Research
Smartphone and social media use among teens is near universal and frequent.
Data
shows teens receive an average of 237 notifications on their phone a day. We know phones are not only a distraction for the owner of the phone, but the entire class is disrupted by the constant ringing, buzzing, and checking of these devices.  This not only results in learning loss for students, but it creates a frustrating environment for educators who try to maintain focus and order in the classroom.
Between 2010-2015, the percent of U.S. teens with smart phones rose
from 23%
to
73%
, with a quarter admitting to being online
“almost constantly”
. Now, teens spend an average of
nearly 8 hours
on screens per day, the equivalent of a full-time job.
Smartphone and social media use contributes to poor mental health, physical health, and academic outcomes in teens.
45% of teens reported feeling overwhelmed by the drama on social media and 26% reported feeling worse about their own lives (
Pew Research Center, 2018
).
Nearly half of U.S. teens aged 13-17 reported experiencing cyberbullying at least once (
Pew Research, 2022
).
There has been a
steep decline in mental health
in children since the early 2010s:
Rates of depression among teens increased around 150% (
American Psychological Association, 2018
)
Suicide rate for kids ages 10-14 tripled between 2007 and 2021 (
Centers for Disease Control, 2023
).
Suicide rate for girls ages 10-14 rose 131% from 2010 to 2019 (
Centers for Disease Control, 2023
).
Sleep patterns also changed during that time, with more and more teens reporting less sleep and
studies showing
that access to and use of mobile devices before bed were significantly associated with inadequate sleep quantity, poor sleep quality, and excessive daytime sleepiness.
In 2012,
math and reading scores
dropped for the first time in 25 years, beginning a downward trend that
continues today
.
In addition to the emotional, physical, and academic toll that excessive smartphone and social media use has on our children, behavioral issues have also increased in the form of
cyberbullying
and costly pranks.
The addictive qualities of smartphones and social media apps have an even worse impact on young children.
A new study published in the
Journal of Human Development and Capabilities
found that children who receive smartphones before the age of 13 were significantly more likely to experience serious mental health problems in early adulthood including aggression, emotional instability, and suicidal thoughts.
Yet the average age for a
child to have a smartphone
in Pennsylvania is reportedly 10.5, a number that seems to get younger every year.
Parents and teachers are worried and want change.
74% of U.S. adults say they would support banning middle and high school students from using cellphones during class, up from 68% last fall (
Pew Research Center, 2025
).
72% of US high school teachers say cellphone distraction is a major problem in the classroom (
Pew Research Center, 2024
).
90% of teachers support prohibiting the use of phones during instructional time (
National Education Association poll from 2024
).
75% of teachers support a bell-to-bell ban, which prohibits the use of cellphones from the first bell of the school day until the last bell of the school day (
National Education Association poll from 2024
).
Cellphone restrictions during school hours free kids from the constant distractions, and can even improve their social interactions, academic performance, and mental health.
Studies
show
cellphone restrictions in school have a positive impact on academic performance, and many students say restrictions have
improved their mental health
.
Anecdotally, schools across Pennsylvania that have already moved to enact restrictions on cellphones during school hours report that students are
interacting more during free time
and
paying closer attention in class
once the distraction of the cellphones are removed.
Learn more about the risks of childhood smartphone use from local advocacy group
PA Unplugged
.

title: Environmental Clean Up & Responsibility Act
raw_text:
Environmental Clean Up
and
Responsibility Act
About
Upper Makefield Leak
The Problem
The Solution
Support ECRA
About
Upper Makefield Leak
The Problem
The Solution
Support ECRA
The Pennsylvania Constitution guarantees all Pennsylvanians the right to clean water. However, current state law does not allow the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection to step in when hazardous spills occur in residential communities and clean ups by polluters are largely voluntary. The Pennsylvania Environmental Cleanup and Recovery Act (ECRA) would make clean up mandatory, fast and transparent for residents, and empower DEP to recover the cost of clean up from polluters through strict joint and severable liability. The polluter, not the taxpayer, must pay for environmental cleanup.
Upper Makefield Pipeline Timeline
Over one year after a jet fuel pipeline leak contaminated private wells in Upper Makefield Township, causing water in residents’ homes to smell like petroleum. After a year of community meetings, letters, and demands for accountability from Sunoco/Energy Transfer, the owners of the pipeline, families are still waiting for full answers and remediation. This spill exposed a major gap in Pennsylvania law when environmental contamination happens in
residential, non-industrial areas
.
Upper Makefield Sunoco Pipeline Leak Timeline
Why have our current laws failed the residents of Upper Makefield?
The sad reality is if the Upper Makefield pipeline leak had happened just two miles to the east in New Jersey residents would have had access to much stronger state government protections. ECRA is based on the New Jersey Spill Act, one of the strongest spill-response laws in the country.
Currently, in Pennsylvania the laws governing hazardous spills include the Hazardous Sites Clean Up Act and Act 2. The Hazardous Sites Clean Up Act was designed to clean up landfills and industrial facilities, not residential areas. Act 2 was intended to clean up industrial sites and provide liability insurance for those cleaning up the sites so they could get cleaned up quickly and back into the economy. Clean up is largely voluntary and these laws are designed for redevelopment, not emergencies where families’ clean drinking water is at risk.
Residents in Upper Makefield have been left in limbo while polluters debate responsibility and remediation plans. Under our current laws, the outcome has been delayed action, uncertainty, and eroded public trust. We cannot allow this to happen in another community.
What would ECRA change for Pennsylvanians facing a hazardous spill near their homes?
If passed and signed into law ECRA would:
Z
Require immediate action
when hazardous substances are released, including containment, investigation, and cleanup.
Z
Make cleanup mandatory
, not optional, when residents are at risk.
Z
Hold polluters fully accountable
through strict, joint-and-several liability so taxpayers are not left footing the bill.
Z
Guarantee residential-level cleanup standards
, protecting drinking water, soil, and air for unrestricted residential use.
Z
Empower DEP to act decisively
, including stepping in immediately when responsible parties fail to act or time is critical.
Z
Create enforceable timelines
so communities are not left waiting indefinitely.
Z
Strengthen funding and accountability
by directing penalties and cost recoveries into the Hazardous Sites Cleanup Fund.
Z
Ensure transparency
, requiring a public-facing portal so residents can track cleanup progress and understand risks.
No Pennsylvanian should have to wonder whether their drinking water is safe while lawyers debate process. Environmental emergencies require
speed, clarity, and accountability
, not voluntary compliance.  ECRA would put residents first and restores confidence that the law will protect communities when it matters most.
How can you support ECRA?
We need your help to get ECRA to the Governor’s desk and make sure all Pennsylvanians are protected from hazardous spills in residential areas. Take a look at our Advocacy Guide for ideas on how you can promote ECRA and get other legislators on our side. We’ve also provided social media posts you can use to let others in your communities know about ECRA. Finally, please sign our petition to support ECRA and make your voice heard!

title: Support Bryan’s Law
raw_text:
Support Bryan’s Law
Bryan’s Law is bi-partisan legislation I am co-sponsoring with Senator Camera Bartolotta (R-46) to
help families of first responders
who die by suicide as a consequence of Post-Traumatic Stress Injury from their line of duty experiences.
Our first responders are heroes who put their lives on the line every day to protect the people of this Commonwealth, and we owe them and their families a debt of gratitude. Too often, our first responders are deeply affected by the horrors and tragedies they witness on the job, but do not receive the help they need. When our first responders fall, in the line of duty or by suicide as a consequence of the weight of their experience in the line of duty, it is our moral obligation to step up and
support their families with the death benefits they deserve
.
Senate Bill 110, Bryan’s Law, is named for Trooper Bryan Gray, a Pennsylvania State Trooper and former Green Beret, who lived in Lower Makefield Township with his family.  The bill has the strong support of many professional organizations supporting our first responders across the commonwealth including the PA State Fraternal Order of Police, the Ambulance Association of Pennsylvania, the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association and the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association.

raw_text:
Farm to School Grant Program​
The Pennsylvania Farm to School Grant Program will provide elementary schools with funding to improve access to healthy, local foods and increase agriculture education opportunities for pre-kindergarten through fifth grade.
The program aims to enrich the connection communities have with fresh, healthy food and local producers by changing food purchasing and education practices at schools and early childhood education sites.

Uses
Project scopes could include the following:
Procuring and marketing local agricultural products into the cafeterias of the schools
Agriculture and nutrition curricula executed at the schools
Agriculture and nutrition incorporated into curricula already present at the schools
Training educators to implement or incorporate agriculture and nutrition curricula into their instruction
Experiential education opportunities regarding agriculture. such as farm field trips, service-learning opportunities on farms (for example, planting, weeding or harvesting), and school gardens
Where applicable
, projects should include:
A list of Pennsylvania farmers who have agreed to supply the school with products from their farms
Nutrition and agriculture education, including integration into regular classroom subjects
Training of teachers and other educational staff on nutrition and agriculture education
Inclusion of parents, caregivers, and community groups in educational activities
Field trips to Pennsylvania farms or other direct agricultural experiences that teach children about sources of food and Pennsylvania agriculture
Eligibility & Funding
Any school district, charter school, or private school with pre-kindergarten classes, kindergarten, or elementary through fifth grade is eligible to apply for up to $15,000.  Preschool programs operated by schools and child care centers are encouraged to apply, but family and group child care homes are not eligible at this time.
Limitations
$500,000 is available for the Pennsylvania Farm-to-School Grant Program; grants will be awarded on a funds-available basis.
Projects must be completed no later than June 30, 2021
Grants will be funded as reimbursement grants
A single grant shall be limited to 75% of the cost of the project
Each school may receive no more than $15,000 annually
Recipients may use the value of in-kind support to match the amount granted

Anglers looking forward to Pennsylvania’s popular spring trout season have another tool at their fingertips, as the

he trout stocking schedule is searchable by county, lists the waterways in alphabetical order, and indicates stocking dates, meeting locations for volunteers, and the species of trout that are planned to be stocked at each location.  In 2025, Pennsylvania’s statewide Opening Day of Trout Season will be held on Saturday, April 5.  A single, statewide Mentored Youth Trout Day will take place on Saturday, March 29.

Stocked Trout Waters
from February 17 to 8 a.m. on the opening day of trout season (April 5), with the exception of the Mentored Youth Trout Fishing Day (March 29), unless waters are included in the Stocked Trout Waters Open to Year-Round Fishing program.

The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission regulates the many essential utility services that Commonwealth residents and businesses rely on every day. State Senator Steve Santarsiero introduces legislation establishing an Office of Manufactured Housing Ombudsman.

BUCKS COUNTY, PA – State Senator Steve Santarsiero (D-10) will introduce legislation establishing an Office of Manufactured Housing Ombudsman to help Pennsylvania manufactured home residents understand their rights and resolve disputes with community owners.
Sen. Santarsiero's legislation, Senate Bill 1446, will serve as a Senate companion to House Bill 2098, sponsored by Rep. Joe Ciresi (D-146) and co-sponsored by Rep. Tim Brennan (D-29), which would establish an Office of Manufactured Home Ombudsman and a Manufactured Home Hearing Board.
The legislation would provide residents and community owners with a dedicated process for resolving disputes involving lot rent, community rules, leases, residency approvals, evictions, and other issues affecting manufactured home communities. The proposed office would also educate residents about their rights and address environmental, health and safety concerns.

"Manufactured home communities provide an important path to affordable homeownership for Pennsylvanians, but residents can face difficult disputes with community owners while having few places to turn for help," said Sen. Santarsiero. "Many manufactured homeowners own their home but lease the land it sits on, leaving them with nowhere to turn when landowners hike their rent unfairly. Our legislation would give manufactured homeowners a dedicated resource to understand their rights, resolve disputes and ensure that their concerns receive a fair and impartial review. We need to make sure that people who have invested their savings in their homes have meaningful protections and a voice when decisions affecting their communities are made."
The legislation is particularly relevant in Bucks County, where manufactured housing communities such as Buckingham Springs provide homes to hundreds of residents. In August, the offices of Sen. Santarsiero and Rep. Brennan met with roughly 200 Buckingham Springs residents to discuss proposed legislation and hear directly about their experiences as manufactured homeowners.

Residents shared concerns about rising lot rents, transparency and the challenges they face when disputes arise with community owners.
"Too many residents are struggling to keep up with steep and repeated lot rent increases, and the General Assembly needs to step up and make sure people who have worked hard to own their homes are not priced out of them," said Bob Besecker of the Coalition of Manufactured Home Communities of Pennsylvania. "The Coalition views SB 1446 favorably because this bill will help our state government protect the rights of manufactured homeowners through an Ombudsman. However, with only 11 legislative session days left in the 2025-2026 legislative session, the Senate must act on House Bill 1250, which is currently awaiting action in the Senate Urban Affairs and Housing Committee, and continue advancing the comprehensive protections manufactured home residents deserve."
"We've invested our hard-earned money into this community — we own and care for our homes, check in on our neighbors, and pay our taxes," said Ingrid, a Buckingham Springs resident. "But our peace of mind is being destroyed by predatory corporate greed. These companies offer zero transparency into how these arbitrary, ridiculous rate hikes are calculated, and they are actively pricing hardworking residents right out of their homes in an already tough economy. We need accountability, predictability, and transparency."
Sen. Santarsiero said the Ombudsman legislation is one part of a broader effort to strengthen protections for manufactured home residents in Pennsylvania.
House Bill 1250, sponsored by Rep. Liz Hanbidge (D-61), would establish protections related to rent and fee increases, disclosure of fees, resident associations and group meetings. The bill passed the House by a bipartisan vote of 144-59 on June 10, 2025, and was referred to the Senate Urban Affairs and Housing Committee on June 18, 2025. Rep. Brennan is a co-sponsor of the legislation and voted for the bill in the House.
House Bill 843, sponsored by Rep. Joe Webster (D-150) and cosponsored by Rep. Brennan, would allow residents of manufactured home communities to purchase their community when the owner seeks to sell. The Senate version, Senate Bill 746 sponsored by Senator Judy Schwank (D-11), is still in committee. Sen. Santarsiero is a co-sponsor of SB746.
“I’ve spoken with many residents at Buckingham Springs about these concerns, especially over the past year, and what stays with me is how much uncertainty they’re being asked to live with. These are seniors on fixed incomes who chose their homes because they believed they had found a place they could afford and stay for the rest of their lives,” Rep. Brennan said. “What also stands out is how much these neighbors look out for one another, supporting each other through the stress of not knowing whether they’ll be able to remain in their own homes.”
“This is a problem we need to address quickly, given the seriousness of the consequences. We’re seeing people in fear of losing their homes because, right now, the state doesn’t provide us the means to protect them. No one, especially seniors, should be at the mercy of unrestricted corporate excess and rules that change on a landlord’s whim,” Rep. Brennan continued. “People who planned responsibly for their future should not have to worry about losing their homes because someone else sees them as an unguarded resource from whom they can squeeze out every last dollar.”
Sen. Santarsiero said advancing HB 1250 remains an important priority as the current legislative session approaches its conclusion. He and Rep. Brennan sent a letter to McKee Villages, the owner of Buckingham Springs, explaining the contents of HB 1250 and asking them to voluntarily comply with the bill before it is enacted into law to protect residents.
"When Rep. Brennan and I met with Buckingham Springs residents this summer, we heard firsthand about the challenges manufactured homeowners are facing," said Sen. Santarsiero. "Those conversations reinforced the need for an Ombudsman who can help residents understand their rights and resolve disputes, but they also made clear that we need broader protections and rent stabilization for residents now. With just 11 legislative session days remaining, we need to move forward on HB 1250 and the other legislation that can give manufactured homeowners greater transparency, stability and a voice in decisions affecting their homes. McKee Villages, the owner of Buckingham Springs, can also act before legislation is passed to be more transparent and fairer to residents now and I hope that they do so."

Credit: Norfolk Southern
Two area lawmakers are calling on federal regulators to halt consideration of a proposed $85 billion transcontinental rail merger until environmental and safety evaluations can be completed.
Advertisements
State Sen. Steve Santarsiero and state Rep. Jim Prokopiak, both Democrats, submitted comments to the federal Surface Transportation Board (STB) on Monday, according to a joint statement.
They are asking the federal Surface Transportation Board to pause consideration of the merits of Union Pacific’s proposed acquisition of Norfolk Southern. Santarsiero and Prokopiak want a full environmental review and have raised questions about safety, infrastructure, and federal oversight.
The STB has authority over the proposed merger and is conducting an environmental review through its Office of Environmental Analysis.
Advertisements
Pennsylvania regulators do not have the authority to approve or reject the proposed merger, as that authority rests with federal authorities.
The regulatory board said in August that the environmental review would include preparation of an Environmental Impact Statement under federal environmental laws.
The proposed combination of the railroads was announced in July 2025.
If approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a single rail system covering approximately 50,000 miles across 43 states, according to the STB.
Advertisements
The companies said Tuesday that the merger would preserve union jobs, lower costs for cross-country transportation and reduce handoffs that can slow shipments. They also said competitors would have to “up their game and compete at a higher level.”
In Bucks County, Santarsiero and Prokopiak are focused on the Morrisville Line and the Morrisville rail facilities.
Based on an STB map, the portion of the Morrisville Line running through Falls Township exceeds the board’s threshold requiring an air-quality analysis, according to the lawmakers. They added that they are also concerned about potential effects on other municipalities in their district served by Norfolk Southern lines that do not exceed the threshold.
Projections submitted by Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern show that by the fifth year after the transaction, freight volume on the Morrisville Line would increase 51.1 percent, from 221.85 million to 335.10 million gross ton-miles.
Advertisements
Truck traffic tied to the Morrisville Intermodal Terminal on Cabot Boulevard is projected to rise by 105 trucks per day, from about 322 to 427.
Annual hazardous-material loads on the Morrisville Line are projected to increase more than 150 percent, from 3,106 to 7,838.
“These projections raise serious questions about what this merger could mean for the safety and quality of life of Bucks County communities,” Santarsiero said. “If we are going to see substantially more freight, hazardous materials and truck traffic moving through our communities, we need to understand the impacts and make sure necessary safeguards are in place if this merger moves forward.”
Advertisements
The STB should complete a comprehensive review of the merger’s effects on Lower Bucks County before considering the proposal, Prokopiak said.
“The Surface Transportation Board must ensure that the proposed merger would not negatively impact residents or businesses,” Prokopiak stated.
State Rep. Jim Prokopiak speaking.
Credit: Tom Sofield/LevittownNow.com
The lawmakers are requesting the STB to figure out what hazardous materials could be transported through Falls Township and examine the potential impacts of a derailment or other release of hazardous materials into the environment.
The two also want the board to determine whether local emergency responders have the training, equipment, and information required to respond to an incident involving hazardous materials.
Advertisements
The projected increase in truck traffic also prompted concerns about congestion, noise, emissions, and traffic safety on local roads.
Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern project that the number of trains on the Morrisville Line would remain approximately the same even as freight volume increases by more than 50 percent.
Advertisements
Santarsiero and Prokopiak said in their statement that it raises concerns about whether trains could become longer or heavier and what that could mean for rail safety and wait times at crossings.
The companies’ projections identify numerous Pennsylvania rail segments and facilities that could exceed STB thresholds for environmental review. The companies have proposed transaction-related capital improvements in 17 states, but none in Pennsylvania, according to the lawmakers.
Advertisements
“We need to know whether Pennsylvania’s existing rail infrastructure, terminals and surrounding roads can safely handle these projected increases, and whether additional costs will ultimately fall on state and local taxpayers,” Santarsiero said. “If improvements or additional emergency-response resources are needed, those needs should be identified and addressed as part of the merger review.”
State Sen. Steve Santarsiero talking to reporters.
Credit: PA Internet News Service
The lawmakers also raised concerns about federal safety oversight for railroads.
Advertisements
The Federal Railroad Administration’s fiscal 2027 budget justification projects staffing of 833 full-time-equivalent employees, down from 947 in fiscal 2025. The figures do not indicate how many inspectors would oversee the Morrisville corridor specifically.
“Before the consideration of this merger moves forward, we need a clear answer about who will be responsible for overseeing this increased activity, whether there will be enough inspectors and resources, and how hazardous-material traffic will be monitored,” Santarsiero said.
Advertisements
The next major deadline in the regulatory process is Sept. 30, when notices of intent to participate are due. Comments, protests, requests for conditions and evidence opposing or qualifying the merger application are due Nov. 18.
The STB has not yet set a date for the public hearing, and a decision on the massive merger could come next year.

“I’ve spoken with many residents at Buckingham Springs about these concerns, especially over the past year, and what stays with me is how much uncertainty they’re being asked to live with. These are seniors on fixed incomes who chose their homes because they believed they had found a place they could afford and stay for the rest of their lives,” Rep. Brennan said. “What also stands out is how much these neighbors look out for one another, supporting each other through the stress of not knowing whether they’ll be able to remain in their own homes.”
“This is a problem we need to address quickly, given the seriousness of the consequences. We’re seeing people in fear of losing their homes because, right now, the state doesn’t provide us the means to protect them. No one, especially seniors, should be at the mercy of unrestricted corporate excess and rules that change on a landlord’s whim,” Rep. Brennan continued. “People who planned responsibly for their future should not have to worry about losing their homes because someone else sees them as an unguarded resource from whom they can squeeze out every last dollar.”
Sen. Santarsiero said advancing HB 1250 remains an important priority as the current legislative session approaches its conclusion. He and Rep. Brennan sent a letter to McKee Villages, the owner of Buckingham Springs, explaining the contents of HB 1250 and asking them to voluntarily comply with the bill before it is enacted into law to protect residents.
“When Rep. Brennan and I met with Buckingham Springs residents this summer, we heard firsthand about the challenges manufactured homeowners are facing,” said Sen. Santarsiero. “Those conversations reinforced the need for an Ombudsman who can help residents understand their rights and resolve disputes, but they also made clear that we need broader protections and rent stabilization for residents now. With just 11 legislative session days remaining, we need to move forward on HB 1250 and the other legislation that can give manufactured homeowners greater transparency, stability and a voice in decisions affecting their homes. McKee Villages, the owner of Buckingham Springs, can also act before legislation is passed to be more transparent and fairer to residents now and I hope that they do so.”

NEWTOWN TOWNSHIP, PA— After years of planning and overcoming challenges, construction of a new pedestrian bridge between Newtown Borough and Newtown Township is a go.
On Wednesday, the Newtown Township Board of Supervisors unanimously accepted a bid from Road Con, Inc. of West Chester to build the Newtown Creek Pedestrian Bridge linking Frost Lane in Newtown Borough with North Sycamore Street (behind Penn Community Bank) in Newtown Township.
Construction will include the bridge, pathways to the bridge from the township and the borough, and fencing and landscaping along adjacent properties. The project is expected to be completed in 2027.

The project will provide a safe, recreational connection across Newtown Creek, fill in a missing link in the local and county trail system, and provide a safer alternative for walkers and bikers to cross the creek.
The project is being funded by three state grants totaling $1,130,000, secured with the major support of State Sen. Steve Santarsiero and State Rep. Perry Warren.

“The addition of a pedestrian bridge over Newtown Creek will not only bridge two municipalities together, but will improve our local and regional trail connectivity,” said Santarsiero.
A rendering showing the walkway approach to the bridge from Sycamore Street. (Howell Engineering)
The piers of the old trolley bridge looking across the Newtown Creek from Sycamore Street. (Jeff Werner/Patch)
A photo showing the original trolley bridge. (Newtown Creek Coalition)
“The Newtown Creek Pedestrian Bridge is near and dear to my heart,” added Rep. Warren. “This bridge will connect communities, both physically and metaphorically, as Newtown Borough residents and Newtown Township residents on 'the other side of the creek' will have safe pedestrian access to the Sycamore Street commercial and business district, and all residents will have another recreational area to enjoy. Thank you to the Newtown Creek Coalition for its vision for this project and its effort in moving it toward fruition.”
The bridge — a joint project between the Newtown Creek Coalition, Newtown Township, and Newtown Borough — will be built next to the historic stone piers of the Old Trolley Bridge, over which an electric trolley ran from Bristol to Doylestown.
The trolley line was discontinued in 1923. It had once traversed Penn Street and State Street before crossing the creek at Frost Lane and continuing its journey to Doylestown.
Designed by Howell Engineering of West Chester, the new bridge will emulate late 19th-,century wooden railroad bridges, according to the Newtown Creek Coalition. The new bridge will be approximately 170 feet long, with paved approaches through wooded areas.
Utilizing natural materials, the project is designed to blend into its surroundings. Wire mesh railing on the bridge will minimize obstruction of the views from the bridge and the creek banks.
Built into the plan will be pedestrian overlooks on the bridge offering views of the creek and the adjacent stone piers. Subtle path lighting will provide safety at night.
The Newtown Creek Coalition is actively seeking funding for additional project enhancements, including benches on the bridge, a landscaped seating area, a path leading down to the creek’s edge, and educational signage.

title: Senator Steve Santarsiero and Representative Jim Prokopiak Call for a Pause on Consideration of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Merger by the Surface Transportation Board until Environmental Review is Finished and Shared with the Public

Senator Steve Santarsiero and Representative Jim Prokopiak Call for a Pause on Consideration of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Merger by the Surface Transportation Board until Environmental Review is Finished and Shared with the Public
September 22, 2026
BUCKS COUNTY – September 22, 2026 −
State Senator Steve Santarsiero (D-10) and State Representative Jim Prokopiak (D-140) are calling on the federal Surface Transportation Board (STB), which has the authority to reject or approve railway mergers, to pause consideration of the merits of Union Pacific’s proposed acquisition of Norfolk Southern until a full environmental impact study is completed and questions about rail safety, infrastructure and federal oversight are answered. They are requesting that the result of the environmental impact study be promptly shared with the public.
Senator Santarsiero and Rep. Prokopiak submitted public comments to the Surface Transportation Board on September 21
st
outlining concerns about the projected increase in freight and truck traffic in Bucks County, particularly along the Morrisville Line and at the Morrisville rail facilities. Based on the map provided by the Surface Transportation Board, the rail segment of the Morrisville Line that runs through Falls Township exceeds the board’s threshold that requires air quality analysis. The legislators are concerned that this merger may impact other municipalities in the district that also have Norfolk Southern lines that do not exceed the board’s threshold as well.
According to projections submitted by the companies, by the fifth year following the transaction:
Freight volume on the Morrisville Line would
increase by
51.1%
, from 221.85 million to 335.10 million gross ton-miles.
Truck traffic associated with the Morrisville Intermodal Terminal on Cabot Boulevard would
increase by
105 trucks per day
, from approximately 322 to 427.
Annual hazardous-material carloads on the Morrisville Line would
increase
more than 150% from
3,106 to 7,838.
“These projections raise serious questions about what this merger could mean for the safety and quality of life of Bucks County communities,” said Senator Santarsiero. “If we are going to see substantially more freight, hazardous materials and truck traffic moving through our communities, we need to understand the impacts and make sure necessary safeguards are in place if this merger moves forward.”
“Any consideration of the proposed merger of Norfolk Southern and Union Pacific should only occur after a comprehensive review of the impact to the Lower Bucks community,” said Representative Prokopiak. “The Surface Transportation Board must ensure that the proposed merger would not negatively impact residents or businesses.”
Senator Santarsiero and Rep. Prokopiak are asking the Surface Transportation Board to examine what hazardous materials would be transported through Falls Township, the potential consequences of a derailment or other release of hazardous materials into the environment, and whether local emergency responders have the training, equipment and information necessary to respond to an incident.
They are also asking the board to examine the effects of the projected increase in truck traffic on local roads, including congestion, noise, emissions and roadway safety. Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern project that the number of trains on the Morrisville Line would remain approximately the same even as freight volume increases by more than 50%, raising questions about whether trains would become longer or heavier and what that could mean for rail safety and wait times at crossings.
The concerns extend beyond Bucks County. The companies’ projections identify numerous Pennsylvania rail segments and facilities that would exceed the STB’s environmental-review thresholds. At the same time, the companies have proposed transaction-related capital improvements in 17 states, but none in Pennsylvania.
“We need to know whether Pennsylvania’s existing rail infrastructure, terminals and surrounding roads can safely handle these projected increases, and whether additional costs will ultimately fall on state and local taxpayers,” said Senator Santarsiero. “If improvements or additional emergency-response resources are needed, those needs should be identified and addressed as part of the merger review.”
They also raised concerns about federal rail-safety oversight. The Federal Railroad Administration’s FY 2027 budget justification projects staffing of 833 full-time-equivalent employees, down from 947 in FY 2025. While those figures do not indicate how many inspectors would oversee the Morrisville corridor specifically, Santarsiero said the projected increase in freight and hazardous-material traffic warrants a clear plan for federal oversight and federal staffing cuts under the Trump Administration lead to serious concern that these trains will be appropriately inspected.
“Before the consideration of this merger moves forward, we need a clear answer about who will be responsible for overseeing this increased activity, whether there will be enough inspectors and resources, and how hazardous-material traffic will be monitored,” said Senator Santarsiero. “Bucks County residents should not be expected to absorb substantially more freight and hazardous-material traffic without knowing that our infrastructure, emergency response and federal regulators are prepared to handle it safely.”
Pennsylvania does not have the authority to approve or reject the proposed merger. That decision rests with the STB. Santarsiero is asking the Board to place consideration of the merger’s merits on hold while their Office of Environmental Analysis completes a full Environmental Impact Statement, and federal safety agencies develop a clear oversight plan.
Senator Santarsiero and Rep. Prokopiak are also asking the Board to identify necessary infrastructure improvements, emergency-response support and other mitigation measures and make any required protections enforceable conditions in the case of an approval.
TIMELINE TO DATE
July 30, 2025 – The applicants (Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern) notified the Surface Transportation Board that they intended to seek approval for the merger.
December 19, 2025 – The applicants filed their original application.
January 16, 2026 – The Board rejected the application as incomplete.
April 30, 2026 – The applicants filed a revised application.
May 28, 2026 – The Board accepted the revised application for consideration, required additional information, determined that an Environmental Impact Statement would be prepared and held the proceedings in abeyance.
July 27, 2026 – The applicants filed supplemental information and revised traffic projections.
August 18, 2026 – The Board lifted the abeyance and set the current schedule.
August 19, 2026 – The Office of Environmental Analysis sent preliminary consultation letters to agencies, Tribes and elected officials, including our offices.
September 18, 2026 – Senator Santarsiero and Rep. Prokopiak submitted preliminary comments to the Board.
September 21, 2026 – Preliminary environmental comments were due.
NEXT STEPS
September 30, 2026 – Notice of Intent to Participate is due. The Board extended this deadline from September 4.
Date not set – OEA will publish its Environmental Notice of Intent and open the scoping process. Public meetings and another comment period will follow.
November 18, 2026 – Comments, protests, requests for conditions and evidence opposing or qualifying the merger application are due.
December 3, 2026 – Preliminary comments from the U.S. Department of Justice and U.S. Department of Transportation are due.
February 16, 2027 – The applicants’ responses and rebuttal are due.
March 29, 2027 – Rebuttals concerning responsive applications are due. This date mainly applies to competing or alternative transaction proposals.
Date not set – The Board will hold a public hearing and issue separate participation instructions.
May 28, 2027 – Final briefs are due.
Date not set – The Board will close the record after the hearing and any additional submissions it requires. The Board states that it will aim to decide the case within 90 days after the record closes, but only if the environmental review is complete.
###

Their comments cite company-provided projections showing freight volume on the Morrisville Line in Bucks County would increase over 51%, hazardous-material carloads would more than double, and daily truck traffic would grow by 105 trips within five years of the merger. They are requesting the board examine infrastructure capacity, emergency responder readiness, hazardous material risks, and federal railroad inspection staffing before proceeding.

title: $2.6M In Grants Coming To Doylestown Area Projects, Institutions
raw_text:
Community Corner
$2.6M In Grants Coming To Doylestown Area Projects, Institutions
Nine community projects and institutions are sharing more than $2.6 million in grants from the state,  announced local lawmakers.
Jeff Werner
,
Patch Staff
Posted
Mon, Sep  21, 2026 at 5:13 am ET
|

Mon, Sep  21, 2026 at 5:16 am ET
The Moravian Pottery and Tile Works has been awarded a $400,000 grant to install radiant heat flooring.
(Jeff Werner/Patch)
DOYLESTOWN, PA — Nine projects and community agencies and institutions in the Doylestown area will benefit from the latest round of state grants coming out of Harrisburg.
State Senator Steve Santarsiero and State Rep. Tim Brennan have announced the following Local Share Account grants for public safety, infrastructure, and community improvement projects:
$900,000 for the Midway Volunteer Fire Company in Buckingham Township for a new fire engine
$433,092 for the PA Biotech Center to renovate and expand its conference area
$400,000 for The Moravian Tile Works to install radiant heat flooring
$100,000 for the Doylestown American Legion Post 210 for kitchen upgrades
$150,000 for the Central Bucks Regional Police Department for portable radios
$35,000 for Doylestown Hospital to purchase a courier van
$46,589 for the Oscar Hammerstein Museum and Theater Education Center to make safety improvements at Highland Farm in Doylestown Township
$425,000 for River Crossing YMCA for the Doylestown Skatepark Revitalization Project
$150,000 for the Doylestown Township Police Department for portable radios and a drone
Biotechnology Center
The Bucks County Biotechnology Center will use its grant to expand a conference room inside of its building located in Buckingham Township.

The life science incubator is dedicated to the creation of a world-class biotechnology center for economic development, job creation, education, and training. The center also provides building space to nonprofit organizations and community groups at no cost to facilitate meetings, events, and essential services.

The center plans to renovate 3,000 square feet of existing conference rooms, undersized kitchenette, and underutilized offices into a flexible, multi-purpose community meeting hub.
“The Biotechnology Center in Buckingham has long been not only a local but national leader in launching new technologies and companies that are creating jobs and saving lives in the life science sector,” said Senator Santarsiero. “This funding will help them improve their conference facilities, which they also share with other local nonprofit organizations.”
Added Rep. Brennan, “The Bucks County Biotech Center is more than a center for cutting-edge research. This investment will create new, flexible spaces designed to bring people together to learn, collaborate and build new opportunities. It will help expand the center’s role as a hub for innovation, community, and economic growth right here in Bucks County.”
Moravian Tile Works
The Moravian Tile Works in Doylestown will use its grant to install radiant floor heating at the historic Tile Works, a living history museum that has produced tiles since its founding.
Tile Works officials say the building’s mechanical systems and its patchwork of electric and gas space heaters are inadequate to support visitation and programming during the colder winter months. They plan to install a hydronic radiant floor heating system that will provide higher levels of comfort on cold winter days to visitors.
“This investment in radiant floor heating will help ensure that the Moravian Pottery & Tile Works can continue welcoming visitors and providing educational programming throughout the year,” said Senator Santarsiero. “The Tile Works is an important part of Doylestown’s history and a unique place where people can experience the arts and crafts traditions that have been part of our community for generations.”
American Legion Post
American Legion Post 210 in Doylestown Borough will use its grant to update the building's outdated kitchen from the 1930s to meet modern safety and building codes. The current kitchen lacks proper ventilation and fire suppression, requiring a full gut renovation to remain functional for veterans and community events. Planned upgrades include new flooring, walls, ceilings, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, and a code-compliant hood and suppression system. The project will also install commercial-grade appliances to support Post 210’s broader effort to revitalize the facility and strengthen its role as a community and veteran hub.
“Organizations like American Legion Post 210 play an important role in bringing veterans and the broader community together, but maintaining an older facility can be a real challenge,” said Senator Santarsiero. “This investment will give Post 210 a safe, modern kitchen that can better serve veterans and residents at community events for years to come.”
Oscar Hammerstein Museum
The Oscar Hammerstein Museum and Theatre Education Center in Doylestown Township will use its grant to address safety hazards at Highland Farm, the historic home of Oscar Hammerstein II, which now serves as a museum and theatre education center.
The project will add a professionally installed safety cover to the historic pool, reconstruct the deteriorated pool house as a nonfunctional decorative structure, and remove the crumbling tennis court to restore safe, accessible grounds.
The improvements will eliminate safety hazards, preserve the property's historic character, and allow the museum to better host school groups, families, and community events, expanding access to the site.
Highland Farm in Doylestown Township.
“Highland Farm where visitors can learn about the life and legacy of Oscar Hammerstein II is an important part of Bucks County’s cultural history,” said Senator Santarsiero. “By addressing these safety hazards, we can help ensure that Highland Farm can continue welcoming school groups, families and community members and sharing this important piece of our local history with future generations.”
“Preserving our history doesn’t stop at keeping old buildings standing. Smart preservation efforts make sure we can continue to use these unique places that helped build our communities, enjoying them and passing them along from generation to generation,” Rep. Brennan said.
“At Moravian Tileworks, that means making the building able to be enjoyed comfortably by visitors and tourists through the coldest months. At American Legion Post 210, it means renovating the kitchen so it can remain a safe gathering place for servicemembers who rely on it for camaraderie and companionship,” Rep. Brennan continued. “And at the Oscar Hammerstein Museum & Theatre Education Center, it means fixing the safety hazards and making other necessary renovations to the building so the people who staff it can keep sharing the important history of its namesake.”
Doylestown Hospital
Doylestown Hospital will use its grant to purchase a courier van. One of the hospital vans currently used to transport medications, medical specimens, and medical supplies at Penn Medicine Doylestown Health is aging and unreliable and a replacement is needed.
“Supporting the infrastructure behind our healthcare system is an investment in the health and well-being of our community,” said Senator Santarsiero. “This investment will help Doylestown Hospital make sure that medications, medical specimens and supplies can get where they need to go safely and efficiently.”
River Crossing YMCA
The River Crossing YMCA will use its grant for a skatepark renovation project in Doylestown Township. The project will involve the revitalization of the Doylestown Y Skate Park. The skatepark has served the community for decades through open skate sessions, day camps, and as the home of the local high school skate club.
The project includes demolition of the existing structure and installation of a new steel skatepark, elements, and fencing. The completion of this project will allow the community to benefit from the skatepark for decades to come.
“The Doylestown Y Skate Park has been a place where generations of young people have come together to skate, learn new skills and build community,” said Senator Santarsiero. “This investment will give the park a new lease on life, creating a safe and modern space for skaters in Doylestown for years to come. Recreation spaces are worthwhile investments that make our communities healthier and happier.”
“Public service takes many forms, and sometimes the most important investments are those that allow an institution to keep showing up for its community. Doylestown Hospital’s new courier van will keep their essential operations moving. Renovating the skatepark at the Doylestown Y will keep it safe and welcoming for young people who need somewhere to gather and have fun together,” Rep. Brennan said.
“These are very different projects, but they share a common thread: they’re investments into the spaces where neighbors can learn, gather, and care for one another,” Rep. Brennan continued.
Central Bucks Regional Police
The Central Bucks Regional Police Department will use its grant to purchase portable radios for use in the three communities it serves - Doylestown Borough, Chalfont Borough, and New Britain Borough.
The department is currently experiencing service issues related to outdated portable radio communication devices that its officers use to communicate internally and with Bucks County. The communication radios are 12 years old and do not provide a supportive signal, which leads to interrupted service and poses safety concerns for the officers and the public.
The Central Bucks Regional Police Department.
“Reliable communication is essential for keeping our police officers and the public safe,” said Senator Santarsiero. “Our officers need dependable equipment, especially when responding to an emergency. This investment will replace outdated radios and help ensure officers have the tools they need to do their jobs safely and effectively.”
Doylestown Township Police
The Doylestown Township Police Department will use its grant for the purchase of 30 portable handheld radios, a drone, and associated accessories. The police department's current radios are at the end of their life and are no longer repairable. The drone will be used to assist with crowd surveillance and improve the accuracy of accident diagrams and scene reconstruction without putting victims or officers in further danger.
“Having reliable equipment is essential for our police officers to do their jobs safely and effectively,” said Senator Santarsiero. “These new radios will ensure Doylestown Township officers can communicate reliably when responding to emergencies, while the drone will give them another tool to assess scenes and document accidents without putting officers or the public at additional risk on busy roads. This investment will strengthen public safety and give our local police the equipment they need to serve our community.”
“Good police work has always depended on good judgment, and today it also depends greatly on having the right tools. Modern radios and drones can give officers better information when they need it – and they give the public greater confidence in how tense moments are handled, building trust between police departments and the public they serve,” Rep. Brennan said.
“I’m glad to see the state making modern tools available to the officers in our communities who are asked to make difficult decisions in high-stress moments. And I’m grateful to the officers who put these tools to work in service of your family, mine, and our neighbors,” Rep. Brennan continued.”
Midway Volunteer Fire Company
The Midway Volunteer Fire Company will use its grant to purchase a fire engine for use in Buckingham Township. At 19 and 29 years old, both engines owned by the fire company are beyond their service life and require significant ongoing repairs and downtime. They are no longer capable of providing the highest quality fire protection services and they are ultimately unsafe not only for the members as drivers and passengers, but for the community at large.
The fire company plans to replace both outdated and unsafe engines with a new compliant rescue engine. The fire company plans to purchase a new apparatus with a six-person cab, 1,000-gallon tank, 1,500 GPM pump, and 60 gallons of foam. It will also be equipped with an adequate supply hose, six preconnected attack lines, and space for rescue tools.
“Residents rely on local fire companies to keep them safe, and our fire companies need updated vehicles and tools to do their job,” said Senator Santarsiero. “I will always support funding for our heroic first responders, like the firefighters at Midway Volunteer Fire Company, to make sure they have the equipment they need to serve our communities as safely as possible.”

Farry and Hogan’s offices said the Bucks County Redevelopment Authority will get $314,384 to purchase 44 hospital beds for St. Mary Medical Center in Middletown Township.

“These projects support key municipal and healthcare improvements, making our community a safer and stronger place to live for everyone who chooses to make the 142
nd

Senator Steve Santarsiero and Bucks County State Representatives Announce $1,800,000 in Grants for Housing and Education Projects
September 15, 2026
BUCKS COUNTY – September 15, 2026
− Senator Steve Santarsiero (D-10) along with Representatives Jim Prokopiak (D-140), Tina Davis (D-141), Brian Munroe (D-144), and Perry Warren (D-29) announced today ­­­­­
$
1,800,000
in state funding:
$1,000,000 for Habitat for Humanity of Bucks County for the Bucks County Blight Abatement Project
$800,000 for Bucks County Technical School Authority for Technical High School Welding and Machining Program Expansion
Habitat for Humanity of Bucks County, Inc. and the Bucks County Redevelopment Authority will use the grant to acquire, remediate, and redevelop 7–12 vacant or blighted properties in Bristol Borough, Bristol Township, Morrisville, and Warminster to create permanently affordable homes through the Habitat Bucks Land Trust model. Using a three-tier acquisition strategy, condemnation, tax/judicial/repository sales, and private or developer partnerships, the project targets both blight removal and expansion of affordable housing. Grant funds will be used exclusively for property acquisition, guided by certified appraisals and strategic selection to grow the Land Trust pipeline. Habitat Bucks will rehabilitate or build homes that meet safety and affordability standards, ensuring long term, equity building ownership opportunities for low and moderate income families.
“Habitat for Humanity of Bucks County has helped change the lives of so many families in our area by making homeownership possible,” said Senator Santarsiero. “All of the properties remediated through this grant will also enter the Habitat Bucks Land Trust model. Each family that buys one of these new homes leases the land from Habitat for Humanity and then later can resell their home to another income qualified buyer while still realizing part of the appreciation from when they originally purchased the home. This creates a permanent stock of affordable housing in our area, turning once blighted properties into community assets.”
“Expanding access to affordable housing and strengthening the welding and machining programs at Bucks County Technical High School will help ensure that more residents have access to the stable housing and skilled-trade opportunities that are critical to our local economy,” said Representative Davis.
“The LSA grants that were awarded today help secure access to affordable housing and skilled-trade pathways here in Bucks County,” said Representative Prokopiak. “These investments are not only essential, but also the right thing to do.”
“I am incredibly proud to support this effort towards expanding affordable housing in Bucks County,” said Representative Munroe.  “It is our responsibility to ensure Pennsylvania families aren’t priced out of their own communities and have the opportunity to put down roots and build a future here.”
The Bucks County Technical School Authority will use state funds for welding lab expansion and a retrofit project to modernize their welding and machining program in the Bucks County Technical High School located in Bristol Township, Bucks County. Their Welding and Machining programs are two high-demand, skilled-trade pathways that are essential to students every year. The school receives over 800 total applications annually but only have space to admit 400 students across all programs. To address these shortages, this project will expand capacity by 100 students per year. This will include 50 additional welding students and 50 additional machining students annually. Improvements will include conversion of existing machining area into a second, fully outfitted welding lab, installation of compliant ventilation and fume-extraction systems, the purchase of modern machining and welding equipment and supplies and associated electrical upgrades, wiring, painting and drilling to retrofit both lab areas.
“Learning trades like welding and machining can set our students up for success in good paying and in demand sectors,” said Senator Santarsiero. “I’m proud to support funding for the expansion of these in-demand programs at Bucks County Technical High School, which does an incredible job preparing our students to succeed in the workforce.”
“For many years applications have exceeded the supply of seats at the Bucks County Technical School, while locally and nationally demand also has exceeded the supply of trained technical workers,” said Representative Warren. “This state local share account grant will help BCTSA address the supply and demand on both ends, by opening up 100 more seats in the welding and machining programs and educating and training 100 more students a year for these in-demand professions.”

title: Senator Steve Santarsiero and Representative Perry Warren Announce Almost $1,500,000 in Grants

Senator Steve Santarsiero and Representative Perry Warren Announce Almost $1,500,000 in Grants
September 15, 2026
BUCKS COUNTY – September 15, 2026 −
Senator Steve Santarsiero (D-10) along with Representative Perry Warren (D-31) announced today
$1,490,000
in state funding:
$200,000 for Lower Makefield Township for the 9/11 Garden of Reflection Renewal Project

The Garden of Reflection 9/11 Memorial serves as a local space for reflection to remember and honor the 2,977 lives lost on 9/11, including 18 residents of Bucks County. After its dedication nearly 20 years ago, the Memorial needs accessibility upgrades and visual improvements. The renovations will include lighting replacements, repairs of uneven walkways and benches, signage and landscaping enhancements, and the restoration of the stonework and fountain pump, which is the focal point of the Memorial.
“This September marks 25 years since the tragic events of 9/11,” said Senator Santarsiero. “These improvements to the Garden of Reflection 9/11 Memorial are crucial to honor the many lives lost, including 18 from Bucks County, and provide the community with a place to reflect on that day and remember our loved ones. This investment will ensure the Memorial remains a beautiful space for the community to gather and remember that fateful day.”
“Last week people from throughout our communities, Bucks County, Pennsylvania and beyond gathered at the 9/11 Garden of Reflection on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks,” said Representative Warren. “Today, we announce the state local share account funding for restoration and improvement of The Official Pennsylvania Memorial to the Victims of the September 11, 2001 Terrorist Attacks. This grant will help ensure that this treasured memorial and park continues to be a place of rest, recreation and remembrance for many years to come.”
The Newtown Fire Company will receive funding to purchase a new ladder truck for use across Newtown Township and Newtown Borough. This apparatus includes updated technology and safety features to enhance both services and firefighter safety to best serve the community.
“Our firefighters shouldn’t need to face unnecessary dangers to their health and safety when they already put their lives on the line to protect our community,” said Senator Santarsiero. “Our firefighters are frontline heroes, and I am proud that this investment will prioritize their safety when responding to emergency situations.”
“The Newtown Fire Association traces its history of service to Newtown to over 200 years ago,” said Representative Warren. “This state local share account grant will help NFA move ahead well into the 21
st
Century with a new, modern, state-of-the-art ladder truck, to continue to protect and serve our community.”
Yardley Borough is receiving funds for the restoration of the borough hall located in Yardley Borough, Bucks County. The borough hall building was built in 1916, and in 1972 when the fire department moved out, the first floor was retrofitted into office spaces for the staff, police, and elected officials. Due to the age of the building, structural repairs, accessibility upgrades, HVAC replacement, and interior modernization improvements are needed for the integrity and structure of the building. Those improvements include waterproofing the basement wall, replacing the windows and doors, installing lighting along walking paths, roof drainage extensions, full depth restoration and grading in the parking lot, replacing the HVAC system, and interior modernization.
“Our local municipalities are hard at work doing the day-to-day work of maintaining our communities, and it’s important that they can do that in a safe and up-to-date facility,” said Senator Santarsiero.” Yardley Borough Hall has served the community for more than a century, and these improvements will help ensure the building remains an accessible and functional home for borough government for years to come. I’m proud to support this investment in Yardley and help our local officials continue providing the services their residents rely on.”
“Local government serves as the grass roots foundation of our democratic system of government, and our borough hall and township buildings are not only the seats of government, but also are gathering places and symbols of our boroughs and towns,” said Representative Warren. “This state local share account grant helps fund the improvement of Yardley Borough Hall, which sits at the center of Yardley Borough, both physically and metaphorically, and serves as a symbol of Yardley Borough and the home of representative government in Yardley.”
